title: Rock Paper Scissors: Decider of Things
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and strategy of rock paper scissors. They open with a note that this is part of a two-part series of children's games with hidden depth (next is tug of war), and an apology for a mix-up with tic tac toe. They cover the basic rules and variations, Takashi Hashiyama's 2005 art-collection auction decided by a rock paper scissors playoff between Christie's and Sotheby's (with the twin-girl advisers), and the ancient-origin question (Egyptian murals, Ming dynasty shushi ling, Japanese sansukumiken games like mushi ken and kitsunken, and jankenpon). They discuss the "rochambeau/rochambo" name and its unclear origin, Nash equilibrium and game theory, the 33.3 percent mixed strategy, the Chinese study on conditional response strategies, professional tournaments and their made-up lore, pre-planned gambits, robot players, and the blindfold study on automatic imitation and mirror neurons. The episode closes with the side-blotched lizard's rock-paper-scissors evolutionary cycle and a listener mail segment about pronouncing Nanaimo and other Canadian place names.

segments.title: Intro and two-part series setup
segments.summary: The hosts explain the episode is part of a two-part series on children's games with hidden depth, following tug of war. They joke about a tic tac toe mix-up with Dave and thank Dave Ruse for help.

segments.title: Basic rules and variations
segments.summary: The hosts explain the basic rules: a count, a simultaneous throw of rock, paper, or scissors, and best-of-three play. They note variations such as counting to four and the way pros hold their hands.

segments.title: Takashi Hashiyama's art auction playoff
segments.summary: Takashi Hashiyama used rock paper scissors to decide between Christie's and Sotheby's for auctioning a roughly twenty million dollar art collection. Christie's recruited eleven-year-old twins Alice and Flora, who advised starting with scissors, and Christie's won by throwing scissors.

segments.title: Ancient origins and Asian precursors
segments.summary: The hosts discuss possible Egyptian origins from murals, the Ming dynasty shushi ling game recorded in Chinese history books, and Japanese hand games like sansukumiken, mushi ken, and kitsunken, along with the Japanese game jankenpon.

segments.title: Even-odd game and arrival in the United States
segments.summary: The hosts compare the even-odd finger game to rock paper scissors and discuss how the game reached the United States, likely through the Pacific Northwest or San Francisco from Japanese and Chinese immigrants. They note that Western writers in the 1920s and 1930s had to explain the rules.
topics: rock paper scissors history in America

segments.title: Rochambo name and linguistic mystery
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why some people call the game rochambo or rochambeau, including a text from Jesse Thorn, a 1930s Oakland handbook spelling, and theories from Japanese or Chinese names. They also mention British and Manchester names for the game.

segments.title: Game theory, Nash equilibrium, and conditional response
segments.summary: The hosts explain Nash equilibrium and why rock paper scissors has only a mixed equilibrium, with a one-third win rate. They describe a large Chinese study that found a conditional response strategy performs better, and note that humans follow patterns and must play quickly.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break before the tournament discussion.

segments.title: Professional tournaments, gambits, and robots
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the mid-2000s tournaments with prize money, the largely made-up lore of the professional rock paper scissors world, pre-planned gambits like the avalanche and bureaucrat, throwing technique, and a robot that can read micro-movements.

segments.title: Blindfold study and automatic imitation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss research on automatic imitation and mirror neurons, where a London study found draws rose when one player could see the other.

segments.title: Side-blotched lizards as rock-paper-scissors evolution
segments.summary: The hosts describe side-blotched lizards with orange, yellow, and blue throats, whose mating strategies form a rock-paper-scissors cycle in evolution.

segments.title: Listener mail: Nanaimo and Canadian place names
segments.summary: A listener from Smithers, BC, corrects Josh's pronunciation of Nanaimo, the cookie bar named after a Vancouver Island city, and notes other tricky Canadian names.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and invite listeners to send mail to the show's email address.
